subject: chemistry
title: Amides
key_idea: An amide has the group –CONH–, a carbonyl joined directly to nitrogen. Amides are made from acyl chlorides with ammonia or an amine. They can be hydrolysed back to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an amine, and they are not basic because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised.

blocks.text: An amide contains a carbonyl group bonded straight to a nitrogen atom. This section covers primary and secondary amides and how to name them.

items.meaning: R–CONH₂: the nitrogen carries two hydrogen atoms, e.g. ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂.
R–CONHR′: the nitrogen carries one hydrocarbon group, e.g. N-methylethanamide, CH₃CONHCH₃.
A prefix such as N-methyl shows that a group is attached to the nitrogen atom, not to the carbon chain.

items: The functional group is C=O joined to N: –CO–NH–.
The name ends in **-amide**. The carbon chain is counted including the C=O carbon.
The same –CONH– link forms the peptide bonds in proteins and the amide links in nylon.
Amides contain a C=O group bonded directly to N.
Primary amides are R–CONH₂; secondary amides are R–CONHR′.
The letter N in a name shows a group on the nitrogen.

blocks.text: Acyl chlorides react at room temperature with ammonia or a primary amine. This section covers the reactions and the reason they work.

blocks.label: Acyl chloride with ammonia
where: The second NH₃ reacts with the HCl produced, forming NH₄Cl

blocks.label: Acyl chloride with a primary amine
where: The second amine molecule reacts with the HCl produced

items: The reaction is a condensation: the molecule HCl is lost when the two molecules join.
The nitrogen lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon of C=O, then chloride leaves (nucleophilic addition–elimination).
It is fast at room temperature because acyl chlorides are very reactive.

diagram.alt: Pick a nitrogen compound to react with ethanoyl chloride and see the amide formed.
diagram.prompt: Pick what reacts with ethanoyl chloride, CH₃COCl, at room temperature.

options.label: Ammonia, NH₃
options.explanation: Two hydrogens remain on the nitrogen.

options.label: Methylamine, CH₃NH₂
options.explanation: The methyl group from the amine sits on the nitrogen.

options.label: Ethylamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂
options.explanation: The ethyl group from the amine sits on the nitrogen.

items: Acyl chloride + ammonia gives a primary amide; + a primary amine gives an N-substituted amide.
Conditions: room temperature, with HCl lost as a by-product.
The N group in the name comes from the amine.

blocks.text: Amides can be hydrolysed back to their parent acid or reduced to an amine. This section covers each reaction.

items: **With aqueous acid** (heated): the amide gives a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt.
**With aqueous alkali** (heated): the amide gives a carboxylate salt and ammonia (or an amine, if the amide is N-substituted).
The C–N bond of the amide group is the one that breaks.

blocks.label: Alkaline hydrolysis of ethanamide
where: Heat with aqueous alkali; ammonia gas is given off

blocks.label: Reduction of an amide
where: The C=O group becomes CH₂ and the product is an amine

items: Hydrolysis with acid or alkali splits the amide into an acid (or its salt) and ammonia or an amine (or its salt).
LiAlH₄ reduces the C=O of an amide, giving an amine.
The same hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds and amide links in polymers.

blocks.text: Amines are weak bases, but amides are much weaker. This section explains the difference using the nitrogen lone pair.

items: The nitrogen lone pair overlaps with the π bond of the neighbouring C=O group and is **delocalised** over N, C and O.
The lone pair is therefore much less available to accept a proton.
Oxygen is electronegative and pulls electron density away from the nitrogen.
Amides give neutral solutions in water. Amines give alkaline solutions.
Amides are much weaker bases than amines.
The N lone pair is delocalised into the C=O group, so it is not available to accept H⁺.

checks.q: Write an equation for the formation of N-methylethanamide from ethanoyl chloride and methylamine, and state the conditions.
checks.a: CH₃COCl + 2CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CONHCH₃ + CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻ (or HCl produced). The reaction takes place at room temperature.

checks.q: Name the products formed when ethanamide is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
Explain why ethanamide is a much weaker base than ethylamine.
checks.a: In ethanamide the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into the C=O group, so it is not readily available to accept a proton. In ethylamine the lone pair is localised on N, and the ethyl group donates electron density, so it is available.
